title: Features of Organisms
page_title: Features of Organisms - IGCSE Biology Revision Notes

blocks.name: The five kingdoms
blocks.definition: State the main features used to place animals and plants into the appropriate kingdoms

blocks.md:
- All living organisms share characteristics. Organisms can be grouped together based on common features they share
- All living organisms can be grouped into one of five kingdoms
- Animals and plants are both kingdoms within this grouping system
- **Main features of all animals:**

  - they are multicellular
  - their cells contain a nucleus but no cell walls or chloroplasts
  - they feed on organic substances made by other living things

blocks.alt: Diagram of a typical animal cell labelled with nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria and ribosomes on rough endoplasmic reticulum
blocks.caption: A typical animal cell

blocks.md:
- **Main features of all plants:**

  - they are multicellular
  - their cells contain a nucleus, chloroplasts and cellulose cell walls
  - they all feed by photosynthesis

blocks.alt: Diagram of a typical plant cell labelled with cell wall, cell membrane, chloroplasts, nucleus, mitochondria, cytoplasm, vacuole and rough ER with ribosomes
blocks.caption: A typical plant cell

blocks.name: The animal kingdom
blocks.definition:
State the main features used to place organisms into groups within the animal kingdom, limited to:
(a) the main groups of vertebrates: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish
(b) the main groups of arthropods: myriapods, insects, arachnids, crustaceans
Classify organisms using the features identified

blocks.md: - Several main features are used to [place organisms into groups](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/1-characteristics-and-classification-of-living-organisms/1-1-characteristics-classification-and-features-of-organisms/1-1-2-concept-and-uses-of-classification-systems/?_ai=internal-linking) within the animal kingdom

- All vertebrates have a **backbone**

  - There are five classes of vertebrates

| Class | Main features | Examples | |---|---|---| | Mammals | - Fur/hair on skin
- Have a placenta
- Young feed on milk from mammary glands
- External ears (pinna) visible
- Endothermic | Horse, dog, squirrel, human | | Birds | - Skin covered in feathers
- Have 2 legs and 2 wings instead of forelimbs
- Lay eggs with hard shells on land
- Have a beak
- Endothermic | Parrot, blue tit, eagle | | Reptiles | - Dry, fixed scales on skin
- Lay eggs with rubbery shells on land | Snake, turtle, iguana | | Amphibians | - Smooth, moist skin
- Adults usually live on land (and so have lungs)
- Larvae live in water (and so have gills)
- Lay eggs without shells in water | Frog, toad, newt | | Fish | - Loose, wet scales on skin
- Use gills to breathe
- Lay eggs without shells in water | Flounder, grouper |

blocks.alt: Diagram showing vertebrate groups—reptiles, fish, amphibians, birds and mammals—with simple notes on skin, eggs, blood temperature and example animals
blocks.caption: Vertebrate classification

blocks.md:
- Invertebrates do not possess a backbone
- One of the morphological characteristics used to classify invertebrates is **whether they have legs or not**
- All invertebrates with **jointed legs** are part of the **arthropod** phylum
- All arthropods share the following visible features:

  - They have an exoskeleton
  - They have a segmented body
  - They have jointed legs
- They are classified further into the following groups:

| Class | Main features | Examples | |---|---|---| | Myriapods | - Body consists of many segments
- Each segment contains at least one pair of jointed legs
- One pair of antennae | Centipede | | Insects | - Three-part body: head, thorax and abdomen
- Adults have six jointed legs
- Two pairs of wings (one or both pairs may be vestigial, meaning non-functional and undeveloped)
- One pair of antennae | Butterfly | | Arachnids | - Two-part body: cephalothorax and abdomen
- Four pairs of jointed legs
- No antennae | Spider | | Crustaceans | - More than four pairs of jointed legs
- Chalky exoskeleton formed from calcium
- Use gills to breathe
- Two pairs of antennae | Crab |

blocks.alt: Diagram showing classification of arthropods into arachnids, crustaceans, insects and myriapods, with simple drawings and key features of each group.
blocks.caption: Arthropod classification

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md:
- Make sure that you are aware of the distinction between the** main features **of a group of organisms and the **defining features** of a group:
- An exam question might ask you to state the *main* features of a group of organisms; these are given above, and some of these main features are **shared between the groups**

  - E.g. all of the vertebrates have a backbone, and all of the arthropods have segmented bodies
- It is also possible that an exam question might ask you to give a *defining* visible feature of any one of these groups, i.e. a feature that **sets a group apart from the other groups**

  - E.g. mammals have fur while the other vertebrates do not, and crustaceans have two pairs of antennae while this is not the case for the other groups of arthropods
- It is common for students to confuse arachnids with crustaceans, and to not be able to state a visible feature identifying an organism as an arthropod, any one of "exoskeleton, jointed legs or segmented body" would be an appropriate answer
